I'm 64 this year, and my back isn't what it used to be. My family holds 5 mu of decent flat land here in Quzhou. I finished middle school back in the 1970s, which was enough to let me read seed packets and fertilizer ratios—more schooling than my father ever had, though these days the young ag-tech promoters talk faster than I can follow. It's early March, and my winter wheat is already in the ground from last October's sowing. I always plant improved wheat varieties from the county station—reliable, not too fancy. I'll top-dress urea when the wheat greens up, irrigate four times total, and spray three times for weeds and rust. I use rotary tillage because I can hire the village machine for cheap; at my age, I don't plough with animals anymore, and my son works in Shijiazhuang so he's not here to help. After harvest in early June, I'll rush-plant summer maize with hybrid seeds—Zhengdan 958 or something similar. Summer is short, so rotary tillage again, two irrigations, two pesticide sprays for stem borers. I thought about planting garlic on one mu for extra cash, but bending to dig garlic kills my back, and vegetable prices swing too much. Grain is safer: the purchase station guarantees a price, and I can always store it in my courtyard if the market is low. So this year, all 5 mu stays wheat and maize. I know I probably use a bit too much nitrogen, but I'd rather lose a little money on extra fertilizer than risk a bad harvest.
